utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. It was scheduled that we would start with the videolink this morning, the cross-examination of Mr. Biscevic. However, there seem to be some technical problems, although the videolink had been tested yesterday. So let's try to use the time as good as possible. I was informed that it might perhaps not take more than ten minutes to restore the videolink. So I'd rather not start a lengthy discussion at this moment on scheduling. But there's another issue I'd like to raise in private session. So, therefore, Madam Registrar, could we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am informed that the videolink is in place at this moment. Mr. Tieger, you're not asking, but you are excused, if ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The videolink is visible on the computer monitor. Good morning, Mr. Biscevic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did hear that you answered to my question but I did not receive any translation of your answer. Or should I go on another --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear the English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now I can hear the English, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness said that he heard you and understood you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then good morning, Mr. Biscevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have been examined on the 6th of September of this year in The Hague, and unfortunately --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- we could then not continue. You could not be cross-examined by the Defence. Therefore, you agreed to be available today. Since it's a long time ago, I'd like you to make again the solemn declaration you already made on the 6th of September that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. So could you please make that solemn declaration now, and perhaps you do it, if -- Madam Registrar, is there a text available in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Thompson in Banja Luka, could you please hand out to the witness the text of the solemn declaration in B/C/S. Then I'll -- yes. Otherwise we could do it in parts. If it could be translated to the witness that -- no. Perhaps we find the ... Mr. Biscevic, you'll see the text of the solemn declaration on the ELMO. If you would please read it and then may I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Biscevic. You'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Stewart --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the Prosecution -- for the Defence, I mean. I apologise. Is there any problem, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There's no problem, Your Honour. It's just a curiosity, really. Don't they get the witness on the screen in the public gallery?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it's for the -- finally, the composition of what is sent out, whether we see the Presiding Judge, Defence counsel, or the witness is governed by specific rules, and the technical booth should make that composition. So at least the witness should appear sooner or later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mainly if he answers questions, whereas usually, if the question is put to a witness, the screen is composed in a way that we'll see the one who asks the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. No. Thank you, Your Honour, for that clarification. I was just interested to know, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- it's of some passing relevance in relation to public nature of videoconferencing evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course. Mr. Biscevic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Stewart, counsel for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. And the public gallery will have to make do with you and me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's -- I have -- I can see it from my -- I can see both that the technical booth has the link picture with Banja Luka. Could I be informed if it would not be possible to include the Banja Luka pictures on the composition. Could I just ask as a test for the technicians, ask them to -- at this moment to show the Banja Luka image on the publicly -- yes. It has been resolved. Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Your Honour, for sorting that out. Cross-examined by Mr. Stewart:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, good morning. Can you hear me there in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning. Yes, I can hear you well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, some weeks ago, when you were giving evidence here in The Hague, you referred to a visit that you described by a number of people, including, you said, Mr. Krajisnik, to Lusci Palanka, around the time that the parties, the SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ, were being formed ahead of the multi-party elections in November 1990. Do you remember that particular point and giving evidence on that particular point?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you identified -- well, you were asked by Mr. Harmon, counsel for the Prosecution: "Now, following the foundation of the SDS party in Sanski Most, did Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Karadzic, come to the municipality of Sanski Most?" And you answered that question. I just want to confirm, Mr. Biscevic: First of all, is it your evidence that you personally saw Mr. Krajisnik in Sanski Most on that occasion in late 1990 -- in Sanski Most, at Lusci Palanka?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the basis of your evidence that Mr. Krajisnik did come on that occasion the photograph that you referred to in your evidence when you were here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, could you give us some guidance as to the transcript pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Your Honour. Yes, this is -- I'm working from the one that has the numbers 5488 and 5489. That's the run of not official, not corrected, as it stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I should have mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, do you need the question again or are you clear enough about what I asked a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm clear about what you've asked me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what is the answer, then, please, Mr. Biscevic?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the multi-party elections were held in Sanski Most, the SDS was established, and when the SDS was established, the first meetings that took place, took place in Lusci Palanka. It was a Serb uni-ethnic local commune, where all the leaders rallied, that is to say, the leaders of the future SDS, from the Federation and from Croatia. There was SAO [Realtime transcript read in error "Savo"] Krajina and from Pristina, there was also support. I myself did not intend personally, but we have a village near Lusci Palanka which was inhabited by the Muslims, and people did go to that meeting, because they didn't think it would be a uni-ethnic rally. And then they told us that they received support from Pristina, from Croatia, and the leaders from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, may I ask you to carefully listen to the question, because the question put to you by Mr. Stewart whether your testimony that Mr. Krajisnik attended was based on the photograph that was shown or, since you testified that you did not personally observe his presence, whether it was on the basis of that photograph that you testified that he was present.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm testifying on the basis of this photograph, and also on the basis of the statements made by the Muslim population who attended the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note it was SAO Krajina, not Savo Krajina, earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, could you be shown, and that will need to be done on the ELMO, as we call it at this end, P115, which is the photograph that we were talking about a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, if you would foresee that you need an exhibit that has been used before, it might be good to have already a small list for the registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I perhaps carelessly only mentioned it to the Prosecution. It's the only one, in fact, anyway, Your Honour. I thought it had been informally discussed, actually, but apologies if the actual number didn't get its way through to Ms. Philpott.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were asked who everybody in that picture was, Mr. Biscevic. The -- you first of all in your evidence - and this was at page 5489, for those who have the transcript at this end - you first of all identified the lady in the picture as Mr. Krajisnik's wife, but you subsequently in your evidence identified that lady as Mr. Karadzic's wife. Just to clarify: Is it your evidence that as far as you recognise the lady, it is Mr. Karadzic's wife?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm just trying to get the photograph back, Your Honour, on the screen. I don't know whether it's dropped off for all of us or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- just for me. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people that you identify there, the second person seated at the table, second from the left, with a beard, apparently, who do you say that is?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Raskovic, from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What degree of certainty do you have that it is Mr. Raskovic?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That doesn't quite answer my question, Mr. Biscevic. There are lots of ways of doing this, like a scale of 1 to 10. But in the first place, I'm just asking you to indicate. You say you think it's him, but that's -- I'll put it this way: You don't know it's him. It could be somebody else altogether; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had any contacts with Mr. Raskovic, but on the basis of the photograph, I concluded that it was indeed Mr. Raskovic. I don't know him closely, so I can't say 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Biscevic, I don't want to have a big debate about the logic of inferring from the photograph itself who it is in the photograph. So let's just stick to something very simple. Do you in fact know whether that is Mr. Raskovic or not?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you don't know?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had any personal contacts with him, so I'm not 100 per cent certain.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you ever seen -- have you ever seen him in your life?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On photographs and on television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you -- or can you date this photograph yourself, Mr. Biscevic?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the beginning of the formation of the SDS, which means sometime in 1990.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not quite my question, Mr. Biscevic. That's your assertion. How do you date that photograph as 1990?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion, the leaders came in from Bosnia-Herzegovina and they lent their support to the formation of the SDS party. They appeared in public before the masses and held fiery speeches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It doesn't answer my question, Mr. Biscevic. Please, concentrate as best you can. What is it -- what information do you have, in the photograph or from outside the photograph, that when you put it together tells you that this photograph was taken in 1990?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was when the leaders were present in Lusci Palanka, when the SDS was under establishment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So does this follow, Mr. Biscevic: That if the leaders were present on some other occasion, the photograph could have been taken on that other occasion?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is also a possibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, I'm not going to beat about the bush any more, Mr. Biscevic. This photograph was taken in 1995, when the Republika Srpska Assembly took place in Sanski Most. Do you know of anything to contradict that assertion that I've just put to you?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't there then, and I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you accept that it is entirely possible that this photograph was taken in 1995?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept the fact that the leaders of the SDS were in Sanski Most, and this is shown on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether the -- yourself, do you know that the Republika Srpska Assembly did hold a session in Sanski Most in 1995?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in Sanski Most at the time, so I don't know. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Raskovic, though alive in 1990, was dead by 1995?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you don't know this, Mr. Biscevic, but do you know that unhappily also Mr. Krajisnik's wife was alive in 1990 but no longer alive in 1995?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said in your evidence that you had voted for Mr. Krajisnik in the multi-party elections. This is at page 5491, Your Honour, of that transcript. And just to remind you, because it's only fair. It was some weeks ago, Mr. Biscevic. You said that -- well, let me ask you this first. Slightly earlier in the transcript, at page 5486, 5487, you were asked, foot at page 5486: "Can you tell me at the republican level who the leader were of the SDS party?" And your answer was: "At the republican level, there was Krajisnik, Karadzic, Biljana Plavsic, and Nikola Koljevic." Now, when you gave that answer, did you understand the question and was your answer relating generally to the period right through to 1992, or were you talking of the time of the multi-party elections only?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The time of the multi-party elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, at the reference which I just gave a moment ago, 5495-491, you had been asked by Mr. Harmon: "Was there an agreement between the parties of the SDS, the HDZ, and the SDA to defeat the communists, and can you describe what that agreement may have been?" That's all in relation to the multi-party elections. And your answer was: "We know that Communism was in power for 50 years in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it was necessary to topple the system somehow. The only way to do so was for the nationalist parties to come together to form an association of a kind, and this is what happened. For example, no one in Sanski Most knew who Mr. Koljevic or Mrs. Plavsic or Mr. Karadzic were. We knew Karadzic. We didn't know who Krajisnik was. We didn't know Mr. Boras or Mr. Ejup Ganic," and so on. So perhaps you could make it clear, Mr. Biscevic. At the time of right up to the actual election, the multi-party election in November 1990, you, you yourself, hadn't knowing anything at all about Mr. Krajisnik, who he was, anything; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as far as you were concerned, at what point did Mr. Krajisnik become - and that was the phrase used in the question put to you - one of the leaders of the SDS party?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to answer?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, I think you can assume that the answer is yes. Whenever I ask a question, please, I would like you to answer, yes.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the parties were formed, the SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ, we contacted -- had contacts on a daily basis, Mr. Raskovic, Ante Turic, and so on. And when the elections were supposed to happen, there was a list with the candidates put forward. And among those candidates were the above-mentioned. We didn't know these people, but we circled their names because that was the agreement we reached. And it was then that Mr. Krajisnik became a leader of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then before the election or then after the election?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until the elections, he was a candidate. After the elections, he was elected and he became an official, a functionary, one of the SDS cadres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You referred to the list and you were asked about it. You said there was an agreement. Mr. Harmon said, this is 5491, line 9: "When you say there was agreement from above and there was a list, what kind of a list was it that you, members of the SDA, received, and what instructions accompanied that list?" And your answer was: "All the parties received it, not only us. There was a complete list of all the parties and it was said on behalf of the SDS that these people have to go through; they had to be encircled." Now, just pausing there, Mr. Biscevic, when you say they had to have been encircled that's what you referred to a moment ago, were you, of -- just on a piece of paper, just putting a ring round their names to identify them; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you continued: "Others for the HDZ. It said don't select anyone from the communist list." And you continued: "How we were to proceed was quite clear and that's how we obtained a majority of votes." And when you say "we obtained a majority of votes," by "we," do you mean all three of those parties together or something else?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all three parties together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then the question you were asked was: "So you were essentially instructed from the SDA party at the national level who to vote for; correct?" Answer: "Yes." Question: "Did that include voting for members of the SDS and the HDZ." Answer from you: "Yes, for all the parties." Question: "Did you personally vote on that occasion?" Your answer: "I did." Were you instructed to vote for Mr. Krajisnik among others?" Your answer: "Yes." "Did you do so?" Your answer: "Yes." Now, Mr. Biscevic, it was impossible for you to vote for Mr. Krajisnik, wasn't it, because Mr. Krajisnik was on the list of candidates for the Sarajevo area, and you were voting in Sanski Most; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you said in your evidence a few weeks ago here in The Hague that you did vote for Mr. Krajisnik, that was incorrect?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDA of Bosnia-Herzegovina voted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you misunderstood the questions, did you, when Mr. Harmon said: "Did you personally vote on that occasion?" And you said: "I did." And then the next question was: "Were you instructed to vote for Mr. Krajisnik, among others?" And you said: "Yes." And you were asked: "Did you do so?" And you said: "Yes." Is it your evidence that you misunderstood that when Mr. Harmon went on to ask: "Were you instructed to vote?", you thought he was no longer asking about you personally, Mr. Biscevic; at that point he had switched to asking about the SDA, generally? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I say that the intention was to vote for the leaders from the SDS. The leaders who were on the list in Sanski Most, and a lot of time has gone by since then, I probably don't know the names, but we did vote for certain leaders who were put forward by the SDS and their names circled and we were told that we should vote for them. The same thing applied to the SDA and the HDZ, from Sanski Most to the Federation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we've got it clear, anyway. You say you voted for candidates in Sanski Most on the Sanski Most list, and that plainly did not include Mr. Krajisnik; agreed?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Biscevic, the voting anyway didn't go quite as you say, did it, because with few exceptions, party voters such as yourself voted for their own party's candidates and not for the other party's candidates?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You disagree?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You -- I just want to clarify a point about census or population figures with you, Mr. Biscevic. At one point in your evidence - and this on the transcript is 5492, line 10 - you said: "Since in Sanski Most the population is multi-ethnic, 40 per cent of Muslims, 42 per cent of Serbs, the SDS Serbian party obtained the majority in Sanski Most." So that's in a nutshell 40 per cent Muslims, 42 per cent Serbs. Earlier in your evidence, just a few pages previously, at 5486, you said, line 15: "In the municipality of Sanski Most, there were various ethnic groups. The Muslims were in the majority, 45 per cent of the population was Muslim, 42 per cent were Serbs, and the rest were Croats or people who had not decided how to declare themselves." Is the -- those are different figures, clearly, Mr. Biscevic. Is the explanation that you were talking in one place about the municipality, the whole municipality of Sanski Most, and in another place about the town of Sanski Most itself?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The latter answer is -- the answer is correct. The former is wrong. The Muslim population numbered 45 per cent, 42 per cent Serbs, the rest were Croats. And when I was talking about the 42 per cent of the Serbs, it was probably the slip of the tongue. So the latter answer is the correct one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it follows that you're saying the former answer is -- well, maybe it's the way -- it's which way around I put it in the questions as opposed to the transcript. Anyway, to get it clear, then, on the basis of the answer you've just given, it was the point in your evidence where you said that 45 per cent of the population was Muslim and 42 per cent were Serbs. That's what you say is the correct answer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, the suggestion I put to you, though, is the -- I suggest to you is the correct one, that for the municipality as a whole, there was a relatively slight Muslim majority, according to the 1991 census, for the town of Sanski Most, it was the other way around, that the Serbs -- there were slightly more Serbs than Muslims. Do you know that? If you can't --

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, you don't know it, or no, you don't agree?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree. There were -- there was not a Serb majority, not even in the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll give you the figures, Mr. Biscevic, because I -- it's probably helpful to do that anyway. For the municipality, according to the 1991 census, Muslims 28.285; Serbs 25.372; for the town, Muslims, 7.377; Serbs, 7.952. But I take it from what you said, please confirm, that you can't give any more information or cast any more light on those figures than you have already said in your evidence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply, I see the difference that you're pointing to. My brother was registered as a Serb, and although he is a Fuad Biscevic, a Muslim, 100 per cent. And there was not one such case but hundreds of them. They were registered in the books as Serbs. And that is why subsequently they were also registered among the Serbs, or kept in the records as Serbs, whereas they were Muslims. And that's why you see that difference there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Biscevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. But may I first ask you a clarification. I missed a bit the point about the 1990 or 1995 picture. Well, I do understand that you said do you know for sure, do you know that person. But then you said, and I don't know how to understand it -- you said this was a picture of 1995; would anything contradict that? Is that -- is it the position of the Defence that the picture was taken in 1995? Because then I have some problems in understanding. If you say: Are you aware that person A was not alive any more, person B was not alive any more in 1995, then I have some difficulties in understanding why it would be 1995 rather than 1990 -- or is it just that you wanted to elicit from the witness that he could not be sure about the date? So is it the position of Defence that it was -- a picture taken in 1995 or that this witness has insufficient basis for any dating?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think somewhere in what I said -- put to this witness, I hope there was, I think there was an assertion that it was 1995. If there's any ambiguity about that, that is the Defence's position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The information about who was alive and who was dead, we've gone as far as we can with the witness as far as evidence is concerned. The -- such matters are then -- well, they're to do with any submissions or argument or inferences that then can be drawn or supported as to the date of the picture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I now -- I think I slowly get your point of those persons -- you made sure that a woman on the picture was a specific woman and not another one who --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if it had been -- well, there's no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Position of the Defence is -- yes. Position of Defence is that it was actually taken in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. And Your Honour it might be helpful if I just say in a nutshell, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course it was important to me to establish with the witness that there wasn't any misunderstanding about the lady in the picture, that it was Mrs. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It could not have been 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course, because unhappily Ms. Krajisnik was no longer alive. It's not to say she would have been in the picture at either date, but then so far as Mr. Raskovic is concerned, of course if it actually is Mr. Raskovic in the picture and it's the Defence's case it's not, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- again it couldn't possibly be 1995 so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's -- okay, now --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- that's where we go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You just excluded some uncertainties which might have opposed against dating this picture in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Particularly as far as this witness's evidence is concerned. But the Defence's case is yes, it was -- it's a picture from the 1995 visit to Sanski Most in connection with the Republika Srpska Assembly. That is the Defence's position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear to me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, is there any need to further -- questions to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Biscevic, you'll now be examined again by Mr. Harmon, counsel for the Prosecution. Re-examined by Mr. Harmon:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Biscevic. Thank you very much for appearing in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning to you too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There has been a question as to the date of the photograph that you have been shown. It is Prosecution Exhibit 115. You testified that you concluded this photograph was from the date when the SDS party was founded. You've based that on both the photograph and on the basis of statements made to you by Bosniaks who attended the rallies associated with the founding of the SDS party. Was it reported to you by members of the Bosniak community on the date and the occasion of the founding of the SDS party that Mr. Krajisnik was in the municipality of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Lusci Palanka, at the time, the SDS had their seat. That's what -- that's when they decided to establish the party, and that's when the representatives from Pristina, Croatia, and other officials were present there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And my question to you was: Was it reported to you by members of the Bosniak community that Mr. Krajisnik attended those meetings and rallies associated with the founding of the SDS party in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you again: The gentleman would come to Sanski Most on numerous occasions later on, but this was a meeting for the establishment of the party in Lusci Palanka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I understood your testimony, Mr. Biscevic, to be this: That at those -- at the founding events associated with the founding of the SDS party in this particular village, members of the Bosniak community attended. They didn't think it was mono-ethnic, these rallies. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Since the village is situated very close to Palanka - Palanka was a local commune - that's why they went there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did those Bosniaks who attended those ceremonies report to you that Mr. Krajisnik was there?

utterances.speaker: FAIK BISCEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. Thank you very much, Mr. Biscevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the Chamber has no questions, so the parties are not asked whether the questions of the Chamber would raise any further issues. Mr. Biscevic, the Chamber has no further questions to you. Therefore, this concludes your testimony. I was tempted to say in this court. Well, you testified in this court, although from a distance, from Banja Luka. Since you explained that it was not easy for you to find time again to further testify, I'd like to thank you very much for having come to Banja Luka and to have answered the questions of the parties. And I hope that you'll have a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the -- Ms. Thompson is the -- I think we could now disconnect the videolink with Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, we have to see what we should do now. And then your next witness, since we have quite some time available, would you be able to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I asked the case manager to make those arrangements right now. We still have the issue of the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we have the issue of the exhibits. We have a few more. How much time do you think it would take for your next witness to arrive, or is he already in the building?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you anticipated too quickly, Mr. Harmon, to -- because I was just discussing what our programme would be today, and I wanted just -- first of all, to know whether there was a witness present at all. But I would suggest, as a matter of fact, that we still have to hear the submissions of the parties on the schedule that was presented by the Chamber. And as I indicated before, that would be one round of each party, ten minutes, and, if needed, another round of each party, five minutes. The Chamber would very much like to hear those submissions first before this break. That would take us 20 minutes for the first round. Then to have a break, and then finish the five minutes for each party after the break, and then hear the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I need to get my papers on that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, we -- Mr. Harmon's got a practical reason which he's just given, but I would also ask to have a break before we do that, because I want to have a chance to have a further discussion with Ms. Loukas about the matter as well. So it seems that for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we could do is to have -- we can do -- to start with the witness at this very moment would be one option, but then he would have to wait for quite some time if we would hear the submissions of the parties on the scheduling after the break. So perhaps it would be better to have the break now, then to have half an hour for any submissions, all together, on the schedule -- the provisional schedule as suggested by the Chamber. Certainly not more. And then hear that witness. That would bring us to -- if we would start at a quarter to 11.00, then at a quarter past 11.00 we would start with the next witness. And if there would be any time remaining, we have to deal with a few exhibits as well. But that's not urgent at this moment, I would say. So if the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, on the question of the exhibits in relation to the last witness, I'm not sure there is really any serious --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The previous witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I was talking about this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were talking about this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The witness coming up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the last witness in the updating we had I think on the 4th of October, but perhaps Madam Registrar you could assist us whether the exhibits tendered in relation to Mr. Biscevic, whether we decided on them.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibits for Mr. Biscevic were admitted on 04/10/04.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And they are exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what I had in my mind, the 4th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think we are again invited not to speak all at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then I suggest that we have a break until a quarter to 11.00, then spend half an hour, not more, on the scheduling issue and that we would start the examination of the next witness, which is an 89(F) witness, as far as understand, at a quarter past 11.00. Yes, it is so decided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The parties have an opportunity now to make any submissions in relation to the suggested provisional schedule, long-term schedule, as presented to them by the Chamber. Mr. Hannis, it's you who is going to address us first?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to start off and tell you where I'm going to end up. Based on our review of the data regarding what we've done so far and what the Court proposes, we're going to suggest to the Court that we think your proposed schedule, we would like to suggest that it may require an additional five or six weeks beyond the 22nd of April. And I'll tell the Court why. Of our 101 viva voce witnesses, Your Honour, my calculations are based on what we had done as of the beginning of this week. Up to that point, we had had 33 of our viva voce witnesses, and we'd had five 92 bis witnesses who were required to come for cross-examination. We used approximately 127 and a half hours for those witnesses, or actually, 128 hours, I guess, Your Honour, which is 22 hours under the one third of our total 450 hours, that one third of our witnesses would take, all other things being equal, if you follow me so far. So I think we are moving more rapidly as we go along, but that's something that we have to take into our calculations. Between the 26th of October, the beginning of this week, and the 22nd of April, 2005, allowing for the Christmas break, for the non-sitting week in November, and the non-sitting weeks in the new year that the Court suggested we would take between the 17th of January and the 22nd of April, I calculated that we would have approximately 85 trial days, which are projected out to 340 hours of court time. Now, discounting time for procedural matters and for cross-exam of 92 bis witnesses, of those 340 hours, if we used them only for direct examination and for cross-examination, at the usual rate of 60 per cent for cross-exam, I calculated that we would have 225 hours for the Prosecution's direct exam and 135 hours for the Defence cross-exam; of the remaining 68 viva voce witnesses. That's subtracting 33 from 101. So far, as I calculate it, our average time on direct examination for the 33 viva voce witnesses that we've had is 3.86 hours. That's higher than the Court's calculations, but I'll explain why. I took 127.4 hours, which was the total direct exam time for those 33 witnesses, and I came out with 3.86. The Chamber average for the witnesses on the list that was given to us was 3.4 hours. But that's because it included the five witnesses, the five 92 bis witnesses who were here for cross. Their total time on direct examination was 0.8 hours for all five of them. So that's -- sort of skews the average a little bit because it was such a small amount of time for the five of them. So if I take that figure of 3.86 hours as the average and I multiply that times the 68 witnesses remaining, I come up with a total of 262.5 hours, approximately, for direct examination. That's approximately 37 and a half hours more than the 225 we would have between now and April 22nd. If you add in the 60 per cent for cross-examination, 60 per cent of that 37 and a half hours is 22 and a half hours. That gives us another 60 additional hours or three weeks of trial time. In addition, I threw into the calculation some amount of time for administrative procedural matters based on our first third of this trial. That was running about 16 and a half per cent of the total time. I guess I was optimistic and figured that could be something less, but I thought that between that additional time that we request for direct and cross-exam of those remaining 68 witnesses and some time for administrative and procedural matters, plus I added in about one week for 92 bis witnesses for cross. Based on the first third of the case where we had five witnesses, their total time on direct exam and cross-examination was approximately 7 and a half hours. If we had five witnesses in the first third of the case, say, we might have ten more in the remaining two thirds of the case, and double the time, 7 and a half hours, 15 hours, maybe 20 hours. So one more week for those witnesses and one or two more weeks for the 16 and a half per cent for administrative procedural matters. That's where I come up with the figure of an additional six weeks beyond April 22nd, which I believe would take us to -- I think that Friday, the first Friday in June is June 2nd, 2005. And that's the end of my calculations, Your Honour, if you have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I do understand that you -- your response is mainly in terms of not objecting to the time of scheduling --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but that you think that calculations should bring you a little bit further in time compared to the calculations that of course are underlying the scheduling as suggested, the provisional scheduling as suggested by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- one more thing about that. The front part of our case, the first third, we called more crime-base witnesses in the first part of the case, partly in response to a Defence request about needing more time to prepare. And although initially on one of our first schedules we had some of our more lengthy witnesses and more substantive witnesses in terms of internationals or experts, we moved some of those farther off. And the witness we had at the beginning of this week, we anticipate we're going to have more witnesses like that, who, as the Court could see, sometimes it takes a little longer to get the evidence from than others. On the other hand, we have learned ways to move faster in introducing our case with Rule 89(F) and 92 bis and we're able to short -- so I'm trying to balance those two things, anticipating that the last part of our case has a greater percentage of our more complex and lengthy witnesses, on the one hand, which would increase the average time per week, but on the other hand we've learned some short cuts and ways to move faster so that's why I felt comfortable in sticking with that average of 3.86 hours, or four hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That answers the only question I would have at this moment, that is whether we approach it in a more dynamic way or in a rather static, statistical way. And I can tell the parties that the Chamber, at least also included some of the dynamics and the developments until now in its calculations underlying the suggestions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And even though with that projected calculation and that requested time, Your Honour, we anticipate that our total time for presenting our case was still going to be maybe 50 hours under the total 450 that were allotted to us at the beginning of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes on the basis of the dynamics the Chamber even thought that it would be still a little bit less than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you may be right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, then it's the first round, the ten minutes for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Two rounds are a knockout, is it? Is that the system, Your Honour? The -- well, of course, that said, Your Honours, we wouldn't start from here anyway in the time-honoured phrase. But just to adopt something of the very twenty-first century terminology of dynamics and statics and so on. In a sense, there is a key distinction there, Your Honour, because what Your Honour was saying, whether we approach it in a more dynamic way or in a rather static, statistic way, now, Your Honour, retrospectively it would be our submission that the Defence's -- sorry, the Trial Chamber's rejection of our motion some months ago was based on a rather arid statistical approach, as opposed to what we would suggest is, wouldn't necessarily use the word dynamics, but something, we would suggest, like the real world as opposed to a calculation of simply hours and figures and so on. Because that is really why we wouldn't start from here. The -- we don't -- we don't quarrel how well Mr. Hannis's figures were followed by the crowds in Banja Luka this morning, but we believe we followed them and see the calculations. So we don't -- we don't quarrel with the figures. We follow those and, in fact they are, joking apart, they are very clearly presented and we see the figures and we see where that leads. Underneath that are one or two additional quite serious problems, which are that when we consider the enormous imposition placed on the Defence in the trial so far, on which Your Honour knows our position and it hasn't changed, the fact that during the first third of the trial we have had more crime-base witnesses, that they take time in a different way, but they aren't, frankly, as inherently difficult to deal with as the other witnesses. The problem is just going to get worse. So we are in a position where this case -- you know, Your Honours know our submissions. This case is at impossible bursting point for the Defence, that the team that we have cannot and has not been able to manage, whatever it may look like on the surface, has not been able to manage this trial effectively so far, and with the change of schedule, and in effect, the increase of dynamic pace, if you like, as opposed to statistical pace of sheer numbers of witnesses, we are going to go beyond bursting point to something which is utterly impossible. So that is our starting point, Your Honour. At some point we are going to have to bring all this back before the Court in a formal way, but the problem is that this schedule won't work because this schedule will be -- will have to explode at some point anyway, because it is a fundamentally a statistics-based schedule which seems also to work to a point -- a point which squeezes everything, and at this -- right here where we are now, which is rather an important point to consider, where we are actually today and where we go from here, which we submit is always a pretty useful test, going somewhere from here, this simply cannot work for the presentation of a fair defence. We're not quarrelling at all with what the Prosecution have said about the need for the presentation of their case. That makes absolute sense. We see that from their standpoint. Your Honour, the -- we would actually like to put a question, if we may, respectfully, to the Trial Chamber, which is important in relation to all of this, which is that: All this draft, proposed, provisional schedule produces an end date for the actual hearings, including evidence and closing arguments of 6th to 7th March 2006, with the judgement then projected for end of April 2006, which necessarily implies that a huge amount of work will have been done on the judgement as the case is proceeding, because clearly it's not contemplating that it gets written from the 7th of March to the end of April. And I don't think there's any secret about that, Your Honour. And I'm -- we're not suggesting that there's anything improper with a judgement being worked on during the case. That's perfectly normal. So please don't misunderstand us in relation to that, Your Honour. But we do ask the question, Your Honour, whether there is a target date that exists anywhere, whether there is a target date which is being , well, imposed, requested, or whether that is the way it's working. Because it does fundamentally make a difference whether there's a target date from which we're working back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me be quite clear on that issue, Mr. Stewart. This scheduling and a target date is not imposed, is not requested, is not anything of the kind, apart from, of course, the general framework, that we all know that the Tribunal, under the Security Council resolutions is required to wind up its work by a certain date. But apart from that generally known information, there's nothing, apart from the thoughts of the Chamber itself, that has led to this schedule. So there's no outside pressure, nor by other chambers, nor by the President of this institution, apart, of course, that we communicate scheduling. But there's never been --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- anything like you should finish by that and that date. It's entirely, I would say, the independent assessment of the Chamber of what could be achieved if we work efficiently on this case and provide a fair trial to the parties. So just to make that quite clear that there's not such a thing as you asked whether there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm very glad to have that assurance, which implies, therefore, that if Your Honours come to the conclusion that more time is needed beyond April 2006 to meet those criteria of efficiency, of course, but fair trial for Mr. Krajisnik, then we will have that time. That's -- that is the -- that is the logical consequence. And we're pleased to have that assurance, Your Honour. So may I, therefore, because Your Honour has invited us to do this pretty quickly this morning, but just running through the draft schedule. Our very brief comments were going to be that close of Prosecution's case 22nd of April, 2005, that was simply too fast. The Prosecution say that's too fast and too soon. We would, as Your Honour knows, we would go further than that, because we say we need a lot more on the Defence side. But in general terms, it's obviously too soon. The gap between close of the Prosecution case and submission of a 98 bis motion is likely to be simply too short. One can't anticipate exactly what the content of that might be, but that is really very short. There's no inherent problem, then, about the timescale of the next few stages, 98 bis motion, response, reply, decision 73 ter conference and so on. We would have made and, in a sense, do make a submission in relation to start of the Defence case on the 11th of July, which is that would be a -- generally too quick, but, B, there would be a problem which we would invite the Defence -- the Trial Chamber to recognise if it should still arise in the light of the Prosecution's submissions, which is that starting the Defence case in the middle of July, which other things being equal and without an absolute firm commitment, we would expect that on the footing that - and I have indicated this with no great secret - on the footing that it is extremely likely that Mr. Krajisnik himself will give evidence, but we would start with him, and it's an unhappy position to have your client in the middle of his evidence at the end of July, over the recess, coming back after the recess. Because he would be that long in evidence. We have no doubt about that if Mr. Krajisnik -- if we were to start the defence case on the 11th of July, we would not finish Mr. Krajisnik's evidence before the recess. So that would be an enormous practical obstacle. We would in any case have said, well, please give us those extra few weeks to have a clean start after the recess. But it may be that that problem, even within the parameters, if I can put it that way, that we're discussing this, as indicated by the Trial Chamber, it may be that that problem doesn't arise anyway. So far as the defence case is concerned, Your Honour, overall, again, the time frame, with that observation about the starting point, the time frame from 11th of July through to 21st of January, that doesn't at the moment strike us as inherently problematic or obviously wrong. That sort of period. It's of course rather early for us to be able to say specifically. But, Your Honour, we don't -- we don't quarrel with the general guideline approach that about 60 per cent of the Prosecution's case or the Defence case is likely to be in the right region and we don't quarrel with the general time frame there. Our problems, as Your Honour indicates, those arise earlier. If the problems are resolved and we have adequate time to deal with the case between now and the start of the defence case, we wouldn't expect by then to have any particular difficulty in meeting that sort of time frame. I hope that's helpful for Your Honour. And the rest, then, final briefs. Well, it's a tight period, but we understand that the tight period between close of defence case and final briefs, if that is coupled with adequate time to prepare and adequate time to deal with the Prosecution case and the presentation of the defence case as we go along, we understand that built into that is the assumption that it's manageable to deal with the preparation of the final briefs in tandem with the conduct of the case so there can be a short period. We don't quarrel that as a proposition. We don't say that there's some magic about having a long, long time after the close of the case to submit closing briefs, provided that at that stage up to the closing of the case there is enough time to be able to do that in tandem. That's really the essential point. Of course we have absolutely nothing to say about the gap between closing arguments and judgement except that I have no doubt everybody would be delighted to have the judgement within that sort of time frame, which is rather quicker than sometimes has been the position. So we would -- we would congratulate and welcome a Trial Chamber producing a judgement in that time period after closing arguments. The tiny observations, Your Honour, are only that the cross-examination being -- the figures calculated for cross-examination at the moment, as 58.9 per cent only just within the guideline in substance, we come rather more within the guideline because those are figures which include the 92 bis and 89(F) witnesses. So in substance we are well within. But my final observation, Your Honour, is this: That Your Honour may have noticed that the cross-examination of Mr. Biscevic this morning was really quite short. Your Honour, that's an illustration of that fairly well-known saying: Well, I apologise for writing such a long letter. I didn't have time to write a short one. Whether it was George Bernard Shaw, whoever it was. Your Honour, there is great efficiency to be achieved by giving people enough time to do things, and sometimes the considerable amount of work that goes into preparation actually has the result that things are refined and we do end up with shorter, tighter, more focused, more concise examination of witnesses. And that's -- that's common experience. Not just in the law; it's common experience in the world. But it is absolutely specific experience in trials and it is demonstrated in this case. There are false economies to be achieved, and only superficial economies to be achieved by too much of a statistical approach to such matters. So, Your Honour, that's our first round of submissions. We hope that that's helpful on the basis of information and an indication as to where the Defence stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You know, Mr. Stewart, in boxing there's a bell that rings after the round is over. I didn't want to ring a bell at this moment, but ... First of all, I'd like to make two short observations. I think you have noticed quite well that the Chamber is not asking the parties to make great effort in keeping this trial within certain time-limits, but that it seeks to contribute to that itself as well. And I think you rightly noticed the short time we allow ourselves for preparing a judgement, not because we'll not take sufficient time to consider all the elements, all the aspects of the case, but since a lot of work can be done already in early stages. Analysis of certain elements of the case can be made, whether they will finally support one solution or another, but the analysis can be made. So therefore, the Chamber is doing exactly the same, at least intends to do exactly the same as it is asking from the parties. Similarly, of course, if you say the 92 bis motion, well, might perhaps need a bit more time, of course the Chamber there also expects the parties to do whatever they can already in those stages. Of course, you can't do it all. You have to take your time when it comes to filing such a motion. But of course, quite a lot of work can be done in earlier stages. And I do understand that you say the more time you give us in preparation, the more time we also have to process all the information. So that's understood. When you said -- where you made the -- some -- where you gave some comments on the dynamics and the statistical ones, I had in mind, as a matter of fact, to make a distinction between dynamic statistical and a static statistical approach. So you're right in saying that both the approaches have a lot of statistics in them. But what I would like to say at the end of this first round, and let's see whether we need a second round, is one of the things that's also of great importance for the Chamber is to give -- of course the parties, but the parties are here in a professional position, but also to give Mr. Krajisnik an idea on how long he would still have to be in this courtroom and how long he would still have to wait for decisions, whether it will be halfway or whether it will be after the presentation of the Defence case. Because the Chamber is aware that it is a burden to sit in court and to go through such a trial, and that it would -- perhaps even more burdensome if you have got no idea when it will end, what the Chamber has in mind as what could be a reasonable time frame for this trial. So that's certainly, apart from efficiency, apart from statistics, is certainly one of the elements that's driving this Chamber to get some control over that and to give some guidance to the parties, to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. accused, and also to itself. We have heard the first-round submissions. I don't know whether there's any need at this moment to go through a second round of five minutes. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.text: There's only one additional thing I want to mention, Your Honour. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, if it is, I hope it's not me that gets knocked out, Your Honour. That's all. The -- the -- yes, well, I just have two brief observations, Your Honour. One is: Yes, we appreciate everything that Your Honour has said about the Trial Chamber's work. There is one very big difference, which is that -- and, Your Honour, here I -- we don't give evidence, but I do sometimes sit as a judge in the high court in England, so I do have some feel of what it's like to have -- not in a case of this size or nature, of course, but one thing which is clear is that if at any point the Trial Chamber feels it hasn't got enough time to work on a judgement and needs more time to work on a judgement, well, the great thing for the Trial Chamber is that you can -- Your Honours can give yourselves more time. So nobody else is ever going to tell you or be able to tell you: This is the time you've got. Because if you need it, of course -- well, it's your duty and responsibility to yourselves and everybody, and Mr. Krajisnik. You can and will take it. And I suppose, Your Honour, that so far as resources can be made available within this building to assist the Trial Chamber to accelerate and meet that deadline, that will happen. Because it's a helpless position to be in, in many ways, and that's obvious, and we see it all the time and we feel it all the time and it's there in all our discussions. So a long stop date for Mr. Krajisnik many, many months later than this would give him what Your Honour referred to just now, but it would also give him an opportunity better to have his defence presented. Your Honour, specific matters in relation to the imminent schedule, but those are rather different. I don't know whether Your Honour wants me to deal with those while I've got my gloves on or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but then we should establish that at this moment we finish. Perhaps is that about November, December?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know. That's difficult. We moved Ms. Hanson once and I -- actually, I think we moved her twice. Once that the Court didn't know about but ... utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, actually, Your Honour, partly -- perhaps I can just answer. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's still to be decided yes.

utterances.text: Which is another issue because actually, Your Honour, we also -- given the stretch of defence resources, I must be frank about it, Your Honour, I do not wish Mr. Krajisnik or anybody else to devote time to witnesses who might or might not be called. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The parties are urgently invited to resolve the one-week problem. We indicated last week that we'd like to have responses on a motion, and since we had not much time left. So the parties are invited to have an intense conversation on that during the next break. Yes. Then the transcripts usually say OTP confers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'll try to discuss that and get back to you before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart is available anyhow, because he didn't intend to stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm at everybody's disposal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know who is going to do that. Do I understand that the next witness, it's Ms. Karagiannakis who will take the next witness. Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just say, I should be in Defence counsel's room for the immediate future and I also have my usual number so the Prosecution can get hold of me easily in the building right now.

utterances.text: Yes, before you leave, Mr. Stewart, I just wanted to inform you that part of the scheduling, just factual information, that seven days, of course, is the term mentioned in the Rules. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Odobasic, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Odobasic, from your answer, I take it that you can hear me in a language you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher and I'd like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Odobasic. Please be seated. Mr. Odobasic, you'll first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution, and after that, you'll be examined by counsel for the Defence. If the Judges would have any additional questions, we'll put them to you as well. There is, however, a specific procedure that a part of the evidence you could give to us will be presented by summarising the relevant parts of earlier statements you have given to the OTP. And then additional questions to that will be put to you. This is just for reasons of efficiency. Ms. Karagiannakis is going to examine you, will explain to you how it works, and you'll then be able to hear that summary. Ms. Karagiannakis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we proceed, there's just a small matter. I can indicate -- perhaps the witness might need to remove his microphones just for the purposes of this initial comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Odobasic, could I ask you just -- first of all, could I ask you: Do you understand any English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please take off your earphones. Very little is not nothing, Ms. Loukas, but ... Could you take off your earphones for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I can indicate that I had certain objections to the statements which, prior to the witness coming today, happily, Ms. Karagiannakis and I have resolved. I think there's just one small outstanding matter, and that is paragraph 62 of the statement. That's paragraph 62 of the ICTY statement dated 30th of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can deal with that at a later stage, you said.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. That's my suggestion, Your Honour, but I think it's important that I alert the Chamber to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could the witness please be provided with the redacted B/C/S version of his ICTY statement dated 30 January 1999 and a number assigned to it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit P362. Examined by Ms. Karagiannakis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Odobasic, do you see your statement in front of you there in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that statement as a statement that you gave to the representatives of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review this statement before today's proceedings?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you advise me of the following two corrections to be made to the statement. The first one is in relation to paragraph 17. I invite you to have a look at that paragraph. Should the first phrase before the comma in that paragraph read: "After the elections and before, during, and after the war in Croatia"? Should that paragraph begin like that?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you also then look at paragraph 46 of your statement. Should the first phrase of that paragraph before the comma read: "From October 1992, they started to take us to working units ..." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: With those two corrections, are you satisfied that these statements are correct and true -- this statement is correct and true?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I now propose to read a summary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: -- of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Odobasic, Ms. Karagiannakis will now read those portions on which no further details are likely to be asked from you. She'll summarise that part of your statement. Please proceed, Ms. Karagiannakis.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: The witness is a lawyer, presently working with the state commission for the tracing of missing persons in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He provides evidence of an SDS rally just before the elections in 1990, in the main square of Prnjavor. The witness had seen both Nemanja Vasic (President of the Municipal Assembly) and Dragan Djuric (President of the local SDS) present at this rally. Radovan Karadzic was also present. One speaker at this rally had urged Serbs to sell their cows and buy rifles. The witness provides evidence about the activities of Veljko Milankovic and the paramilitary group he commanded, the Wolves of Vucjak. During the multi-party elections, this group had the task of appearing at different voting stations to intimidate people, by their presence, into voting for the SDS. Just before or after the elections, the Wolves attacked the main relay station on Kozara mountain and it was turned towards Serbia. During the second half of 1991, the Wolves would often shoot in the direction of Bosniak and Croat houses. The SDS prevailed in the multi-party elections. The SDS replaced general managers and directors who were not Serbs, as well as Serbs who were not members of the SDS. The witness provides evidence regarding the treatment of Muslims and Croats in the municipality. He states that those people who did not answer the call to mobilisation were dismissed from their employment and lost their apartments. Their business premises were destroyed and subsequently taken over by Serbs. During this time, grenades were thrown into the yards of private houses owned by non-Serbs. He observed the armament of Serb civilians. The witness led the local commission tasked with organising the referendum on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina on 29 February and 1st March 1992. The President of the municipality, Vasic, forbade the organisation of the referendum at all locations, except for the Dom of Kultura at the centre of town. In the Croat village of Drenova, several members of the Wolves forced entry to the referendum office and threw documents around. The witness states that the non-Serbs started to leave Prnjavor during 1992 because of mistreatment, looting of property, and forced mobilisation started. Each week, several buses were organised to transport non-Serbs to the Hungarian border. The people had to pay 1.500 Deutschmarks each to leave. Before leaving, the people had to obtain permissions and a paper saying that they were giving their property to Serb authorities. The witness provides evidence on the attacks on the Muslim villages of Lisnja and Puraci. 54 houses were burned down in Lisnja and six people were killed, of which four were boys. The witness states that the Serbs set up a detention camp in the summer of 1992 in the Sloga shoe factory. Several hundred Bosniak males from the villages of Lisnja and Puraci were imprisoned at this detention centre. Serbs had set up another camp at Vijaka, in the mill. Guards at these camps had been policemen and members of paramilitary units. The witness details the evidence of the destruction caused to the mosques, Catholic churches, and the Ukrainian church in the municipality of Prnjavor. And now, Mr. Odobasic, I have some questions to ask you about the details you've given in your ICTY statement. So could you please look at paragraph 4, to begin with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in that paragraph, you note that Prnjavor was a Serb-majority municipality, whereas Prnjavor town had about a three-quarter majority of Bosniaks. You say there, and I quote you: "There were only four other villages inhabited by Bosniaks." Can you please list those villages for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I can. These are the following villages: The village of Lisnja, 12 kilometres away from Prnjavor, in the direction of Banja Luka; the village of Puraci, bordering with the village of Lisnja; the village of Konjuhovci, two kilometres away from the centre of the town; the village of Galjipovci, which is some four to five kilometres away from the town, and there was one another village with a mixed population, not just Bosniaks, but there were Bosniaks, Catholics, and Orthodox people there. This is the village of Babanovci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you please look at paragraph 7. There you state: "At the SDS rally --" you mention a rally and you say: "At the SDS rally I remember that Radovan Karadzic was there, as well as Dusan Zelenbaba, from Knin, who gave a speech, in which he said: Serbs, sell your cows and buy the rifles." Did you actually see this rally and hear this speech?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I was personally present there at the meeting. This rally was held in a city square in front of a shopping mall called Prima, and I was some 50 metres away from the rostrum, listening to what the speakers had to say there at the rally. And I heard Mr. Zelenbaba clearly when he invited Serbs to sell their cows and buy rifles, and without any doubt, this was heard by at least hundreds of other people in Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I draw your attention to statements made in paragraph 9, where you state that a paramilitary unit called the Wolves of Vucjak had been organised and that the leader -- the commander's name was Veljko Milankovic. Then you say, and I quote: "He was well known in the area even before the war as a criminal." Now, what type of criminal activity had Mr. Milankovic been known for before the war?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I am very much familiar with the village that Mr. Milankovic was native from. He was a good-for-nothing person who never had any employment and dealt with -- and committed different crimes. In the period between 1983 and 1987, when I was chief of the town's inspectorate in the town, the forestry inspectorate lady reported him twice for having done petty crimes in the forest. But he was also known for doing a lot of rows, brawls in the village and he was also known for having stolen things, for thefts committed to the people in the town, and I must say that I have known the family of Milankovic for a very long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that paragraph, you go on to talk about his activities in relation to the multi-party elections, and you state: "He blocked the entrance to the culture centre, where a meeting was to be held --"

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to this. If evidence, further evidence is sought to be elicited in relation to this question, I would submit it's preferable not to have the particular paragraph in front of the witness for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I'm happy just to read it to him. He doesn't need to look. I just want to ask the basis for that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.
