You know, Ms. Karagiannakis, in the 89(F), we have developed more or less a rule which says that you can ask the witness either to read or to -- read to the witness what is in his statement, if this is an introduction for further questions. If you seek confirmation of what is in the statement, we would rather not read it, have it not in front of the witness so that you can elicit that from the witness further details on that part.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In fact, I've planned my examination so as to -- so I can put a particular -- parts of his statement not for the purposes of reputation or confirmation but mainly for the purposes of finding out what the basis of what is said in there actually is-- that is his own personal knowledge or something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If we're trying to establish the basis of knowledge, then I take it, Ms. Loukas, that there is no problem in having in front of the witness what he said and of what he's asked.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The distinction that Your Honour has drawn is the distinction that we've all been working to and I just want to ensure that we're proceeding on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Karagiannakis, if you would please keep that in mind, and I leave it up to you whether or not at a certain moment the witness was -- has to be -- has any need to have the statement in front of him. I don't know whether we should take it away now at this moment or whether we can leave it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I think we could just leave it there. And I'll just wait. I'll either read something to him, and if he needs to look at something in particular, I'll invite him to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 9 of your statement, sir, you say: "Veljko Milankovic, and I quote from here: "He blocked the entrance to the culture centre, where the meeting was to be held. He had five or six of his men with him; all of them were armed. He would not let the SDP meeting proceed. He claimed that he wanted to hold an SDS meeting at the same time." Now, what's the basis of your knowledge for that statement?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: As a member of the only multi-ethnic party existing at the time in the territory of the Prnjavor municipality, I was in the executive staff of the party and would go to the rallies, pre-electoral rallies organised by the party, and I'm talking about the SDP. That day we had a rally in the village of Kremna, in the proximity of what was to be the seat of the Wolves from Vucjak and we headed at the culture centre. And there we were -- we met with Veljko, who was there with his Wolves. He was very dismissive, arrogant. He said.. You are not going to hold a meeting here at the culture centre, because we intend to hold an inaugural session of the SDS here. He addressed some of the Serbs who were there, Bijelo Bijelic and others, and said: Shame on you. You're supporting communists. Why don't you join the only Serb party, the SDS --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just stop you, Mr. Odobasic. May I ask you to carefully listen to the question. I mean, what you're saying now is to some extent, although a bit more in detail what appears in your statement. The specific question of Ms. Karagiannakis was: What was the basis of your knowledge. So she'd like to know whether you were there, whether you heard it from someone. This is the question. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was present there and I saw it all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 16 of your statement, you said -- you state: "When the war in Croatia started they used to go to the battlefield and come back with a lot of looted property: Cars and furniture." And there -- in that statement you're referring to the Wolves. Can you please tell the Court how you know that.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I saw it with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown the MUP report, signed by stamped by Stojan Zupljanin, dated 23rd September 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Prosecution Exhibit number P363.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Could the witness -- I think that might be the report that follows that, because the one that I have is certainly longer than one page. So ... I'll give you the ERN. Could the witness be shown both documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next document will be P364.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, could you please have a look at page 3 of the attachment to the first document in B/C/S. It has the number SA 02-0128 on the top of your B/C/S version. Now, there it states that -- this report is speaking about Mr. Milankovic, with whom -- about whom you have stated certain matters in your statement. At that paragraph, it states: "On local and main roads at gun point and in a drunken state, they stopped vehicles and citizens, demanded to see identification papers, conduct searches, insult people and abuse them." Now, do you have any personal knowledge of the Wolves of Vucjak in relation to checkpoints established in Prnjavor municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness's microphone please be switched on.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I did see such checkpoints. I was even stopped at one such checkpoint in a village of Cilasi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you look further down --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you look further down the page on the B/C/S version, beginning of the last paragraph on your page 3. There it states: "Individually as a group, they" - meaning the -- Milankovic and his group - "provoked and harassed the Muslim population with the aim of precipitating interethnic fighting. In the centre of Prnjavor in the presence of a large number of citizens, some of them were aiming their weapons at cars and Muslim individuals." Now, do you have any knowledge of that activity in relation to the Wolves?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: At the side of the road from -- main road from Banja Luka to Prnjavor, I saw many houses that were bullet-riddled and there were many such houses in the town itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that you saw the damage but you didn't actually see them shooting?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I did see on one occasion when a certain member of the Wolves fired shots in the air in the street where I lived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 31 of your statement, you say, and I quote: "The main relay station on Kozara mountain was attacked by the Wolves either just before or just after the elections. And it was turned towards Serbia. The telephones were cut off, the situation of course became worse every day." Now, how do you know -- what is the basis for your statement that the Wolves took over the Kozara mountain relay station?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: This was announced on the media, and generally, there were stories around the town of Prnjavor and certain individuals were really celebrating that event. So it was no secret in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall when this was announced in the media, approximately?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I think it was announced immediately after the takeover of the relay station. I'm not sure. I think it was the radio Sarajevo or some other mass media.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. Could you please approximate the time when you heard that the Kozara relay station had been taken over.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot remember the date, but I think it was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving on to another topic. In paragraph 14 of your statement, you say, and I'll quote you: "All Bosniak policemen were asked to sign a paper swearing their loyalty to the SDS, not to the Republic MUP. Since they did not want to sign such an oath, they were dismissed from the police force." Now, could you tell the Court the basis for that statement?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I personally knew many of the police officers there and I spoke to them. I think one of them was an ethnic Serb and the others were Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the exhibit: "Notice for a court," it's entitled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I think on your version you have a photocopied page of press reports. Could you look at the press report that's entitled "In the public security station Prnjavor. Signing of statement of loyalty has been finished." And then underneath that "notice for a quarter." Could you have a look at that article. Now, that article states that 16 employees of Croatian and Muslim nationality who were members of the collective, that is, the Ministry of the Interior collective in Prnjavor, had refused to sign loyalty. And then it goes on to quote an official about those events. And the quote comes from a person stated here as Radislav Vincic, the head of the public security station in Prnjavor. Now, do you know Radislav Vincic?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I did not know him personally from before, but when he became head of the Prnjavor police station, I read about him and heard about him over the media. I just want to add something to my previous answer. I said I remembered some Bosniaks and one Serb, but I also now remember that there were two Croats who also refused to sign the loyalty oath.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the Radislav Vincic that you've just described as holding the position of -- the head of the public security station, is that the same person as the Radislav Vincic referred to in paragraph 15 of your statement, where you refer to him as the chief of police?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, in paragraph 19 of your statement, do you state, and I'll quote you: "I know that a Serb SDS organiser called Milan Spasojevic told a Bosnian, Esref Softic, that: The time has come for Serbs to finish what we started in the Second World War"? Could you please tell the Court how you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: He said that to my uncle Esref Softic and he told me the very same day what the man had told him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember approximately when you heard about this event?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I think it was -- well, possibly it was in 1991, perhaps towards the end, but I can't remember the exact date. I didn't consider it to be important. But I think it was 1991, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in relation to -- in paragraph 22 of your statement, you say that you observed Serb civilians being armed and I'll give you a quote and ask you a question: "Once I noticed a large truck parked in the front of a hunting lodge near Prnjavor and were distributing weapons to Serb civilians." Now, do you recall when, approximately, you saw this event?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the date now. I think, I say I think, that it was during the war in Croatia. But as I say, I can't be specific.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 23, you say: "Everyone who refused to answer the mobilisation call was dismissed from work and expelled from apartments which were owned by public companies." Now, what do you mean to say -- what do you mean by the phrase "expelled from apartments which were owned by public companies"?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Well, they were apartments who were assigned to -- by the public companies to the employees, to the employees working in those organisations and companies. They would sign contracts, giving them these apartments, and then if somebody would not -- fail to call -- fail to respond to the call-up for mobilisation, they would rescind those contracts, by which they had allotted those flats to them. And then the people would receive documents saying that they had to move out within a deadline.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 26: "One of the very important things which influenced later events was the decision of the Presidency of the Republic Bosniaks did not have to answer the mobilisation call, saying we weren't going to fight against Serbs or Croats. We obeyed this decision not to go to the army, and that's why we had a lot of problems." Now, in that statement, who do you mean by "we"? Who obeyed the decision not to go into the army?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Mostly the Bosniaks, the Croats, and some other people of an ethnic minority. They refused to go and serve the army because that would mean going to the battlefront in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 23, you talk about the treatment of non-Serbs in the municipality. Now, you state there: "They also started taking over all businesses. During this time, grenades were often thrown into the gardens or yards of private houses owned by minorities." Now, who do you mean by "minorities" in that context?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Well, in view of the fact that the Serbs had the absolute majority in the town of Prnjavor, everybody else was a minority and came under that category.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you mean to say the non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: All non-Serbs, yes. Because the majority population were Serbs and 9 per cent were the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You go on --

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: 29 per cent, sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You go on tots that bombings of businesses took place. Now, do you have any knowledge about who bombed the private houses and businesses of non-Serbs in Prnjavor municipality?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I can't confirm that, but the rumours going round town was that it was the members of the Wolves from Vucjak, especially one of their members called Jansa to others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you actually see the destroyed houses and businesses?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Dozens of such businesses and premises, and my business too was seized that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about whether these houses and businesses that were bombed, do you have any knowledge about them being looted as well?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: My business premises were. As to the rest, I can't say. Most probably they were, because it was theft taking over these business premises after the diversions that were created.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did these bombings and -- when did these bombings start happening?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: The bombings -- I'm quite certain that they started in the first half of 1992, and I assume that already towards the end of 1991, there were some such bombings too, diversions of this kind, where grenades were thrown and things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraph 8, you discuss your role in organising the referendum for the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 29th of February and the 1st of March, 1992. You say there that you formed a commission. In that paragraph, you state: "Serbs tried everything to prevent the referendum voting in Prnjavor." Can you explain to the Court what you mean by that. Sorry. It's paragraph 28.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Up -- according to the provisions that were in force the heads of the city commissions were nominated by the commission of Bosnia-Herzegovina and I was appointed president of the commission for the town of Prnjavor. And as such, I was supposed to organise in the local communes and in the various localities electorate boards. And I went to the Municipal Assembly to inform the president of the Prnjavor municipality about that - his name was Mr. Vasic - and tell him we were going to organise a referendum and conduct a referendum, which was something that was done throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. The gentleman was quite explicit and said that the referendum would not be held in Prnjavor. He also said that we couldn't use the places where the elections took place in previous years. And later on, he allowed just one premiss, the culture centre, so that he could see who was coming to vote. All the other voting posts were in private houses or in some religious premises, against the will of the president and the powers that be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What political party did that president belong to?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: He was from the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You go on to describe an incident in that paragraph 28, and I'll read out the relevant portion to you: "Besides the central location we also established locations in the villages close to the mosques. I remember that in a Croat village of Drenova, several persons of the Wolves forced entry into the office of the referendum and threw documents around. When the Croats gathered up the documents -- then the Croats gathered up the documents, withdrew to a nearby field and held the referendum voting there. An international observer arrived in Prnjavor, I went with him to that village and those Wolves left without further damage being done." Now, how are you aware of the -- of that situation prior to arriving at the village and observing what you did?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: As president of the local commission, I had to set up the electoral board. So I went to the village beforehand. And we maintained telephone contacts with the presidents of all the boards and commissions, as well as the one in Drenova. And at one point in time they informed me that that voting post had been attacked. And at the time, with the international observers and a certain parliamentarian, Naim Kadic, from Bosnia-Herzegovina, I went to the spot and really on the route to the voting post, we were indeed stopped by those Wolves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Paragraphs 33 and 34 of your statement, you address the issue of non-Serbs leaving the municipality. In paragraph 34, you say that the Serbs found -- you say: "Each week, several buses were organised to transport Bosniaks -- Bosniak and Croats to the Hungarian border via Serbia, where they were pushed out of the buses and left like cattle. The cost of this drive was 1.500 German marks. Before this trip each person had to obtain seven or eight separate permissions and sign a paper saying that they were giving all their property to the Serb authorities. Now, did you see these buses leaving the municipality?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw them on several occasions. I even sent off some of my own relatives who left in that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many of your relatives left in that way?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: At least ten that I could name, maybe more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: They were mostly Bosniaks, but there were also some Serbs and Croats who left in the same way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned their having to obtain seven or eight separate permissions. What types of permissions did people have to obtain before they left the municipality?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I had to go through that procedure myself later on. Well, you had to have seven or eight permits, and they were as follows: First of all, you had to come by a permit that you weren't being prosecuted in any way. Then later on, a permit that you were not due for military service. And even children of the ages of 2 or 3 and the elderly persons who were not military conscripts had to have permits of this kind. Then you had to have a permit saying you didn't owe money for electricity bills, water bills, telephone bills, et cetera. Anyway, there were seven such permits. Then you would have to go to court to sign a statement saying that upon your departure you were leaving your property to a lawyer to sell within the space of six months, and failing to do that, then the property would come into the possession of Republika Srpska. Only once we had collected all those permits and permissions we would get a permit from the secretary of national defence allowing us to leave, to take the journey taking us to third countries. However, these permits just lasted one month and if you didn't leave within the space of a month, you had to get the permits out again. And each permit cost a certain amount of money. So by the time you got seven or eight of them, this would be a costly business and come to 500 or 600 German marks or more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, paragraph 35 and 36, you describe attacks on the villages of Lisnja and Puraci, which you've told us are Bosnian-ethnicity villages. And you state: "Later on the Serbs attacked the villages of Lisnja and Puraci with military weapons. 54 houses were burned down in Lisnja and six people killed." You also state that Serbs shot four young boys. And then in paragraph 36 you state: "During the attack on Lisnja, they had also shelled and then destroyed with explosives the mosque in that village." Now, how do you know about the events in Lisnja and Puraci?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Well, in Prnjavor, there was great pressure being exerted when this was going on because many people from Lisnja and Puraci escaped to the towns, to find refuge there. And rumours were going round as to what was happening there. And I talked to an eyewitness for a long time, somebody who had seen everything that had been happening in Lisnja. And as far as the killing of these young men is concerned, I know that ex officio, because they were exhumed a month prior to that and they were returned, their bodies returned to the village of Lisnja and that's where they are today.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the bodies of those four boys?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Those young boys, after they had been killed, were transported to the village of Konjuhovci, which is where they were buried, and I myself was in the cemetery several times, standing at the graves of those four young boys. And let me repeat a month ago, the commission I work in received a request to exhume the bodies to establish the cause of death and to take them back to their local villages, that is to say, the village of Lisnja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of the approximate age of those boys?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: They were either minors or thereabouts, very young boys, just before the age of maturity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So do you mean to say that they were teenagers? Younger or older than that?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you actually mean by "teenagers." When I say they were minors and young minors, that implies from 16 to 20, in that age group. Of course, I didn't check it out, but they were young, young boys.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say you spoke to an eyewitness of these events. Can you name that person?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I talked to Miralem Mehimovic [phoen]. I also talked to Nijaz Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to the Muslim population after the attack on the villages?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: As I said, a portion escaped to town and took refuge with their friends and relatives. Most of the men were arrested and taken off to an area which was turned into a camp. It was, in actual fact, an area belonging to the Sloga shoe factory. It was in the town of Prnjavor, opposite the gymnasium, the secondary school there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: That might be an appropriate moment, Your Honours, if we're taking a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it would. Ms. Karagiannakis, would you have any indication on how much time you would still need?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Less than half an hour. In fact, something between 15 minutes and half an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That even, Ms. Loukas, would lead me to see whether, one way or the other, I've got no idea what your cross-examination will be, but whether we could finish with this witness before the weekend. Otherwise he would have to stay for perhaps not more than one hour after the weekend, and that's something the Chamber wants to avoid, to the extent possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, as do I, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Of course, it's not entirely within my hands, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: -- I would have thought that -- well, the witness answers everything the way I want him to, it will be very quick.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: But I'm anxious, Your Honour, to ensure that the witness doesn't have to stay in The Hague over the weekend, and I feel certain that if -- let's see. We're now 20 past 12.00. We'll take a -- I assume, a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Then if Ms. Karagiannakis comes in under her half an hour, I will do everything, I can assure, to -- that we finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we see, Ms. Karagiannakis, if we have a 20 minutes' break now, then if you could try to see whether, by 1.00, you could finish your examination-in-chief. Then we would have 45 minutes remaining for Ms. Loukas. And that, Ms. Loukas, would approximately do -- of course you never can -- but -- always has to ask the Defence whether you're confident that -- yes. I see from your unspoken response that ... Mr. Odobasic, we'll try to see whether we can finish your testimony today, so that it's not necessary for you to, well, spend here the weekend and then -- I don't know, of course, what kind of arrangements are made, but at least that as far as your testimony, it's not necessary, then, to keep you over the weekend. We'll resume at 20 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to turn into private session for a very short moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Odobasic, Ms. Karagiannakis will now resume the examination. Please proceed, Ms. Karagiannakis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Odobasic, before the break you had given evidence about the attacks on the village of -- Muslim villages of Lisnja and Puraci, and you told us who had told you about those attacks, the eyewitnesses. Now, did they tell you anything about who had launched -- who had conducted the attacks on the villages?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I do know for certain that the Wolves of Vucjak took part in it, as well as the regular police force from Prnjavor. And in view of the fact that the village was attacked with heavy artillery being used from a locality called Pavlovo Brdo, then I'm certain that some military units took part as well. I can't say at this point in time whether they were local units or members of the JNA or whatever, but the village was attacked with artillery, weapons, which means weapons that the Wolves of Vucjak didn't possess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In paragraph 38 of your statement, I'll quote you. Now, you say: "I also heard on the radio station a reserve artillery captain named Nedeljko Davidovic, who told her he had 'defeated the balija' by shelling the village and afterwards Wolves units moved in and looted and burned the houses." Now, what village are you referring to in that statement?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Both villages, Lisnja and Puraci, because they're linked on to one another. It's difficult to differentiate between the two and say where one starts and the other end. They follow on from each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the break you also mentioned that the men from Lisnja and Puraci had been taken to be detained at the Sloga shoe factory. In your statement you say that this occurred in the summer of 1992. You also state, and I quote: "They brought in, but not all at one time." And I'm quoting from paragraph 39: "They brought in but not all at one time. Several hundreds Bosniak males from the villages of Lisnja and Puraci." You go on to say: "I was never able to see that camp personally. It didn't exist for long. They interrogated the people, took the money from them, and expelled them from the area. The guards were policemen at that camp." Now, how do you know about these details?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Well, an absurdity happened from what I did previously. I know the facility well, what it looked like inside and out. And as to the events in the camp itself, I was told by Halilovic, Nijaz, who was a civil engineer, and I happened to be his boss beforehand. But somebody else interrogated him, somebody called Vasic Stamenko - I was also his boss - and the other members of the Prnjavor police of the day. So Nijaz Halilovic told me about the events that went on in the camp for the most part and some of my neighbours who were from Lisnja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the following paragraph, 40, you mention a camp at Vijaka and you called it the old mill. And I -- then I'll quote: "They took prisoners from Derventa and only some from Prnjavor. The guards were police and some members of the paramilitary units." Now how did you come to know about these details?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Lokic Bilko, one of my friends, was one of the prisoners who had been badly beaten up in the camp, and there were a certain number of other bogs knack had who passed through that particular camp. But I think that he was maybe for the Croats from Derventa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Karagiannakis, the Chamber highly appreciates the speed you develop, but it might be a bit too much for the transcribers and interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph -- paragraph 27 of your statement, there's no need to look at it, you say -- before I ask the question, could the witness please be shown the next bundle of exhibits or have them before him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, that would be number or numbers ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be P366, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: While the witness is being shown the exhibits, I might identify what they are for the record by reading out the titles. There is a ruling dated 21 July 1992 from the municipal misdemeanours court of Prnjavor municipality, finding -- well -- it is accompanied by a statement of reasons. And then the final document in that bundle is a ruling, a statement of reasons of the municipal misdemeanours court of Prnjavor municipality. And that is dated the 13th of October, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Odobasic, in paragraph 27 of your statement you say: "Because I refused to be mobilised I [sic] started a court procedure against me and I had to pay a fine. I did not pay and they sentenced me to prison for 17 days. I suppose the prisons were already full and I didn't go to the prison on that occasion." Now, does this bundle of documents represent court rulings in respect of proceedings against you for failure to answer the misdemeanour offence of mobilisation? So the misdemeanour offence of failing to obey a mobilisation call.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. These are the rulings that refer to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as you know, were other non-Serb people subjected to these types of legal proceedings in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I think most of them were, most of those who failed to respond to the mobilisation call were, and the rest escaped to third countries, precisely because of this mobilisation call.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your statement, you've detailed acts committed against the non-Serb population of Prnjavor municipality during 1991 and 1992, and they are -- they include the burning of Muslim houses and businesses, the destruction of a number of mosques, the attack on Lisnja and Puraci, and two detention facilities. As far as you know, was Veljko Milankovic or the Wolves of Vucjak or anyone else involved in these acts convicted and punished in the municipal court of Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, nobody was ever punished, and I don't even know if proceedings were initiated in any of these cases either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: That concludes that topic now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about some names that are mentioned in your statement, and could you -- we'll begin with Dragan Djuric. Could you tell us what political party he belonged to.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I think he was one of the founders of the SDS in Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What position did he hold in the municipal government?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I don't think he was in the municipal government. He was in the Republican Assembly as a deputy of the SDS. And I think his -- he received his term of office the first multi-party elections, when they won two mandates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear him make any statements with respect to Muslim people in the municipality of Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: The gentleman very often made unacceptable statements over the radio, and when under the influence of alcohol, in the time itself -- in the town itself, he would not mince his words. For example, when he was a guest at the local radio station, he would always have nationalist songs played from Serbia, to show his political affiliation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that he often made unacceptable statements. Can you tell us what those statements were?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Well, at the beginning, they were a little more moderate, in the sense of saying that a Serbian state would be formed and those who accepted a state of that kind can stay. But later on this took on a different form and shape. And since you mention it, sabotage and diversions started, mistreatment started and persecution started. He personally went to work organisation to see if the non-Serbs, the non-Serb inhabitants of Prnjavor had been dismissed from their jobs. And whether the contracts allotting him apartments had been rescinded and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your last statement you said: "Well, at the beginning they were a little more moderate in the sense of saying that a Serbian state would be formed and those who accepted a state of that kind can stay. But later on this took a different form and shape. Can you tell us what type of statements he makes -- he made later on.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Later on, especially when the events in Lisnja took place, he said that all the Muslim population had to be disarmed and that they had to be loyal; if they were not, then an attack on Lisnja for every Serb head that fell, 100 balija heads would fall, meaning Muslim heads.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just in relation to that aspect of the evidence, I think it would be important to clarify whether this is something he heard himself or heard from others. To date, Ms. Karagiannakis has been ensuring that the witness makes those distinctions, and that last series of questions doesn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although it could have been asked to the witness in cross-examination, I wouldn't mind if you would do it at this moment, Ms. Karagiannakis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The statement that you just told us about in relation to the events in Lisnja, I'll read it to you: "He said that all the Muslim population had to be disarmed and they had to be loyal. If they were not an attack on Lisnja for every Serb head that fell, a hundred balija heads would fall, meaning Muslim heads." Do you hear that personally?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I heard that and some other statements. I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What other statements did you hear personally?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Well, over a local radio broadcast, Mr. Djuric was a guest and he was explaining the establishment of the SAO of Krajina, Bosnian Krajina, and I called in to the broadcast, to the programme, and I said that a district of that kind could not be formed because there were municipalities and 24 of them should have come under that area. And that they could not be formed in which -- in those municipalities where the Bosniaks win the majority. And then he said that they wouldn't be asking the people but that they would implement the decision to form the SAO of Bosanska Krajina and things along those lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say in your statement that Nemanja Vasic was the president of the municipality, and you also say that he's a member of the SDS. Did you ever hear him -- did you ever personally hear him make any statements with respect to non-Serb people in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I heard from other people. That was actually in 1994 that he made a statement that doesn't refer to this case. In the beginning he stated that the Serbs had taken over power, that they would not use any forceful methods to force non-Serbs out of the town. But since he, as president of the municipality, tolerated all these events leading up to the persecuting of non-Serbs, to drive them out of the area, it becomes quite clear that these were just platitudes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any involvement that he had in the dismissal of non-Serb people and non-loyal Serbs in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I do not know whether he was a direct participant in that, but he was the one representing the organs, the authorities, and the organs of the Municipal Assembly did implement the dismissals of people and the evictions from the apartments and he being president of the municipality must have known about it all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What position did Radivoje Radivojevic hold in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: He was president of the Executive Board, meaning the prime minister of the government of the town of Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What political party did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: He belonged to the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear him make any statements with respect to non-Serb people in the Prnjavor municipality?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I did not hear his statements. He was more careful in that respect. I know him well. I used to be his boss for four years. But in his appearance he would wear unacceptable iconography, wearing a beard, something that was associated to the conduct of the previous war criminals, of the war criminals of the previous war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say unacceptable iconography, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the Second World War war criminal that was sentenced to death, to be shot by a firing-squad, Draza Mihajlovic. He wore this type of beard and very small glasses. So this man also wore them, just like this war criminal, and he was actually quite successful in doing so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any involvement that Mr. Radivojevic had with respect to the dismissals of non-Serbs and non-loyal Serb people from municipal positions?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: All the decisions taken by the Municipal Assembly of Prnjavor where the SDS had a majority had to be implemented by the Executive Board. Mr. Radivojevic was president of the board and the organs headed by him, that is the government of the municipality of Prnjavor, was the one to implement all these decisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Karagiannakis. Ms. Loukas, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Odobasic, you'll now be examined by Ms. Loukas who is counsel for the Defence. Cross-examined by Ms. Loukas:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I seem to be having problems with my headphones. Yes. There appear to have been some gremlins in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems if the output is reintroduced in the system again, this is the kind of sound you get. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just said this is what happens in the output from the system is being put through a microphone in again, then that's the --

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last words were more important, that you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I wondered, of course, if it was some sort of anti-Defence conspiracy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, good afternoon, Mr. Odobasic?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Odobasic, I just want to confirm some matters with you. Firstly, just on this question of mobilisation. Of course, the situation was that the Bosniak Muslims didn't respond in the main because Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, the president of Bosnia-Herzegovina, said that Bosniaks should not respond to mobilisation; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course, even in the face of that some Bosniak Muslims did in fact respond to the mobilisation and did become part of the army; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Very few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But nevertheless, there were Bosniak Muslims who did respond to the mobilisation; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Absolutely so, just as there were Serbs in my army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed. Now, the Bosniaks who did in fact -- Bosniak Muslims who did in fact respond to the mobilisation, they, of course, were not dismissed and didn't lose their apartments; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, going on to another topic: It's true to say, is it not, that the largest number of the people who were dismissed were those who refused to respond to mobilisation; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And of course, there was a number of people of Serb ethnicity who were dismissed for the same reason?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just in relation to the police: The issue, of course, there in relation to dismissal from the police that you refer to in your statement, of course, was not, of course, their ethnicity but whether or not they were willing to express their loyalty to the new government; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think, as you've already mentioned, there were Muslims, Bosniak Muslims, who were part of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Now, moving on to some matters contained in your statement. I just want to go to paragraph 10 of your statement. Do you still have your statement in front of you? Now, in paragraph 10, you refer to a priest who held very extreme views. He encouraged people to vote SDS. What do you mean by "extreme views"?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I know the gentleman from my earlier employment. In the very beginning, even before the multi-party system, he was a man holding very extremist positions, in favour of Serbia. At the rallies that he organised, I think this rally was always on the 30th of July, in Potocani. This was before the start of the war. And there were people wearing nationalist Serbian iconography, unacceptable for Bosnia and Hercegovina, would appear. Therefore, people wearing insignia and clothes that were quite unacceptable. And he was known for organising such religious rallies that were then used to promote some political ideas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in relation to -- moving on to another topic - paragraph 17, you indicate there that after the elections, and I think you made some corrections there, before, during, and after the war in Croatia, the SDS replaced all general managers and directors who were not Serbs. Now, just in relation to that, of course, you're aware that, according to the party agreement amongst the parties in power in Bosnia-Herzegovina after the elections, the SDS, SDA, and HDZ, the highest functions went to the party that had the majority in that municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I don't think you're right. You have to specify the functions that you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, firstly, are you aware of that party agreement, the parties in power in Bosnia and Herzegovina, after the election?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: No. No, I'm not aware of this agreement at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware of municipalities where the SDA were in power, had the majority, in fact replacing people with people from their party?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Madam, we are talking about general managers here, not about municipality functionaries. And I'm not aware of this, because the SDA was of such minor presence in my town that it could not really raise its voice at all. I don't know for the other towns. There were no directors, general managers, in the municipal organs, and I believe your question referred to the municipal functionaries, whereas I'm talking about managers, people managing companies. And this agreement, even if it did exist, as you claim, did not refer to managers of businesses, of companies, but rather to the officials, functionaries in the municipality. It is an absurdity that, for instance, the manager of a utility company had to be removed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In any event, you don't know about the party agreement that I'm dealing with; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: No. I belong to a different option and I have no idea about the meetings and the agreements between these three parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we'll move on to another topic. Paragraph 26, where you deal with the question of mobilisation, and the Bosniaks not answering mobilisation call, are you aware of Bosnian Muslims or Bosniak Muslims going to Croatia to fight on the side of the Croatians?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of any Bosniaks from my town who left to Croatia to fight on the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, moving on to another topic. You refer in paragraph 29 to the question of the referendum, and you make the comment there that SDS leaders threatened to take by force the voters lists. Now, is this something that you witnessed yourself or something that you heard about from another or others?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I was told this by Mr. Muharem Halilovic, who was also a member of the electoral board. In fact, the same was done in the village of Drenova, when they had taken the ballot papers there. This by itself indicates that the same thing could have been done in other places as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were told about this, you've indicated, by Muharem Halilovic. Now, this reference to SDS leaders, did this gentleman refer to any particular names?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: It was 12 years ago. I wouldn't be able to remember any names. I don't know who his -- what his sources were, but he was a very well-informed man, because he did hold various decisions in the municipality, even the high-place positions. I think he used to be president of the municipality. He was a very well-informed man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I think you've -- just in relation to, I think, paragraph 39, you've fairly indicated there that, in relation to the Sloga factory, you were never able to see that camp personally; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: No. I clearly said that before the war, these premises where the camp was formed were premises that I was able to see very often, because I was the deputy manager of the Sloga factory. This particular industrial plant was dislocated from the rest, because all the rest were in one place and this one was dislocated. So it was quite appropriate for this. Of course, I knew what the premises were like from before, because for the period during which the people were kept there, nobody was allowed to enter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but of course my question was: Looking at your paragraph 389, you've indicated there that in relation to the Sloga factory you were never able to see that camp personally. I'm not talking about anything that -- I'm not asking but anything prior to the period in history that we're dealing with. I'm just confirming that you've fairly indicated there that you did not see that camp personally. That's all. That's a correct statement, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: No. I did not see the camp from the inside, but the camp was in the centre of the town, in one of the main streets. You could not pass by the centre of the town without seeing the camp being secured by the police officers. It's maybe some 20 to 30 metres away from the -- one of the main streets in the town. So I did pass by the camp, although I did not see it from the inside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you saw the outside of the building; correct? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, similarly, in relation to what's contained in paragraph 40, at Vijaka, which was called the old mill, that, of course, was something you heard about from one of your friends; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, going back to paragraph 9 in your statement. You indicate there that prior to the elections the Serbs had organised a paramilitary unit called Vukovi sa Vucjak, Wolves from Vucjak. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say before the elections, I take it of course you're referring to the elections of November 1990?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've indicated there that -- towards the end of the paragraph, that the Wolves used to wear uniforms in the villages, but they didn't turn up in town in uniform. This is the second-last sentence of the paragraph. And in the very last sentence you indicate: "During the elections, they had the task to appear at different voting stations to intimidate people by their presence into voting for the SDS." That's what you've asserted there in your last paragraph of paragraph -- in your last sentence - sorry - of paragraph 9; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you actually see this?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I myself did not, but, as a member of the electoral board of the SDP, I had access to the premises of the town electoral commission and I was able to see several complaints lodged concerning the conduct of these people, their coming to the polling station, threatening people of other political options. I think there were several dozen such complaints, and members of my party did take part in examining these complaints. Therefore, I was very well informed about their behaviour at the polling stations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've referred there to uniforms. Did you see the uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: It was very difficult to make a distinction between who belonged to whom, and what these uniforms were. However, the town being in the proximity of the Croatian battlefield, there were many uniformed people walking around, and it was difficult for me to say who belonged to which formations that came to town. But I myself, several days ahead of the elections, when we were trying to hold a meeting in the village of Kremna, I saw the Wolves, who were preventing the meeting from being held, wearing these uniforms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you personally saw the Wolves in late 1990; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the village of Kremna, right in front of the community centre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're certain of that?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: There were several hundreds of us, supporters of the SDP. All of us have seen this. There was a near physical conflict between one of the Wolves and two other men, Segic and Bijelic, from our crowd. There was a row and then Segic took our banner, our flag, and led us all to different premises, the premises of a school there, to hold our meeting there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're as certain of this as you are of the other matters you've given in evidence in relation to the SDS?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you're referring to. What do you mean, in relation to the SDS? I came here to tell the truth and to tell what I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're certain about the evidence you've given in relation to the Wolves, just as certain as you are in relation to all the evidence that you've given in relation to today and in your statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Odobasic, the Wolves were not formed until 1991. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether there's a formal date of their establishment, and I have nothing to say about it. We were by the commander of the Wolves and other members of the Wolves driven away from our venue of our meeting, that was in 1989, just before the multi-party elections. I personally recall that in 1989, a person by the name of Slavko Segic, at one of our SDP meetings, claimed to have seen in the vicinity of this community centre of theirs, they held every day drills, practicing shooting from rifles, from RVD's, hand-held rocket launchers, and other weapons that other formations couldn't have. And I saw on that very spot, subsequently, some empty cartridges there. And this can be confirmed by some other members of the hunting club who were there with me. Whether they have a formal date of establishment, I don't know, but they did appear in 1989 and introduced themselves as the Wolves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, moving on to another topic, Mr. Odobasic. Are you aware of the newspaper Glas?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Glas was a newspaper that was -- used to be published in Banja Luka before the war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you aware of an article on the 27th of January, 1992, in the Glas Daily, in relation to a lorry belonging to "10 July" arriving with weapons for Muslims that were distributed in Prnjavor? Are you aware of that article?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: It was a local paper that I had never read. As far as the weapons in Prnjavor are concerned, I never heard of a single inhabitant of Prnjavor as having received weapons, nor did anybody distribute weapons. At last, then, in 1992, one company that dealt with this was headed by a Serb, and I have never heard of a single barrel as having been distributed to a Bosniak. And I cannot believe such a possibility at all, that a lorry full of weapons would be able to come to the centre of Prnjavor and distribute weapons to the Muslims. That is quite an inconceivable thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you were not aware of arming of Bosniak Muslims in the villages of Konjuvici [phoen] and Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: The village of Konjuvici does not exist. And as far as the armaments are concerned, I have no idea about that, because I'm a man who has always hated weapons, even when I arrived in the liberated, free territory, I did -- I performed a job that was not related to weapons in any way. I repeat: I was a member of a party that could not know what was going on at the time. We were social Democrats who were actually marginalised. We did not take part in the government, and I was not even able to be informed or know anything about such goings-on, if there were any.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Odobasic, on another topic: Were you aware prior to the war of departures of Muslim -- of members of the Bosniak Muslim population leaving Prnjavor on their own initiative because they wanted to avoid the mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: You said before the war? Please, could you be more precise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any time prior to the war. At any time prior to April 1992.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Yeah. The Bosniaks were receiving mobilisation call-ups in 1991, and probably some of them did leave. And it was possible to leave the town without taking part in the convoys. But probably some of them fled, having presaged that something was going to happen. Now, as for the earlier period, it was a town that nobody ever left for any reason other than the economic one, because in this general area, there were 11 different ethnicities living together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you aware of a number of people in your municipality of Croat background leaving to avoid the mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: There were very few numbers of Croats in the town itself, and I'm not aware of anyone having left the town. Now, whether anybody left the villages, I wouldn't call Croat villages, but rather Catholic villages, that is something I know nothing of. In any case, all of these villages were outside the town perimeter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of some Croatians, Bosniaks of Croatian background, in your municipality exchanging immovable property with Serbs expelled from Croatia and going there?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: It is quite likely that something like that happened during the war in Croatia. I'm referring to 1991, when the Serbian authorities expelled a man by the name of Blazevic. He used to be up to then the chief of the TO staff. He might have left and exchanged property with someone in Croatia. But that was his private matter and I never saw the man again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are you aware of the White Eagles apologising for their dishonourable behaviour to citizens of both non-Serb and Serb background?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Could you explain what you mean? Do you mean about my beating up -- my having been beaten up? I don't think they apologised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That wasn't my question. My question is: Are you aware of the White Eagles being forced to apologise for their dishonourable behaviour to citizens in your municipality of both non-Serb and Serb background?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether the witness noticed, but your second question was a different one from the first. The first one was about apologies and the second question was about being forced to apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: I see, Your Honour. Perhaps in my haste to ensure that we finish by 1.45 so that the witness doesn't have to spend the weekend in The Hague, perhaps I neglected to use the word force in the first question. But the second question contains the major elements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the question to you now is whether you know anything about White Eagles being forced to apologise for dishonourable behaviour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I know is that after the attack on our houses and our people, after the looting they had conducted that night, the next day they came, led by a commander of theirs, and returned part of the loot. And among that loot was my father's hunting rifle that was broken, and they had seized it the previous night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you aware of measures being taken to seize illegal weapons in Prnjavor and that these measures being taken irrespective of the nationality of the person possessing the weapon?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Madam, that's a farce. It's farcical to say that. They took away weapons that had been legally registered. One day, yes, they did take them away from the Serbs and Bosniaks, but the Serbs were returned their weapons the very next day. And I'm a victim of this kind of conduct on the part of the local police myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you understand that my function is to ask you questions, and that's part of my duty to the Court. You understand that, do you not?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, I understand absolutely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you realise, of course, that neither you nor I will decide this case; that's up to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, and that's the only way to go about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed. And of course, the Judges must hear the answers to your question from both the Prosecution and the Defence?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: And that's what we're doing, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Odobasic, I would prefer that you answered the questions that I must ask you without comments such as "farcical." Do you understand that, Mr. Odobasic?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, but I must be able to understand each of your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just intervene for one second. The question was about measures being taken to seize illegal weapons in Prnjavor. Your answer was that legally obtained and registered weapons were taken and that -- then you gave a lot of comments. The question was about illegal weapons and measures taken against them. So perhaps you -- if you would have focused on that question, well, you could have said you knew about it or you did not know about it. Could you answer that question, whether you know anything about measures being taken to seize illegal weapons in Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: The only thing I know is the case of Lisnja, whereas in Prnjavor, I don't know of a single case; at least, I don't know about it, where illegal weapons were seized.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If Ms. Loukas would like to further explore that, then she'll have an opportunity to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just in relation to the questions of illegal weapons, are you aware of proceedings being brought by the police in relation to illegal weapons against both people of non-Serb background and Serb background? Are you aware of proceedings of that nature?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during this period where you spoke of public lawlessness and buildings being blown up and what have you, there were, of course, buildings belonging to people of a Serb background that were affected as well, were there not?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I just know of one case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in relation to permits for movement, are you aware of permits for movement being issued for citizens' safety that were issued for all people, regardless of whether they were Serb or non-Serb?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I never heard anything about any permits for movement, at least not in my own town.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour. And I think we've come in within the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any need, Ms. Karagiannakis, to put further questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Odobasic, I would have two questions for you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first one: You were asked by Ms. Karagiannakis about the -- about your knowledge of military returning from Croatia with their loot. You answered that you saw it yourself. Could you please clarify for me: If someone uses a car or furniture, how you can see that it's looted rather than obtained in any way other?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Right close to my house there was a close relative of the Wolves' commanders living there and in one day the man brought in 14 carloads with licence plates which testified to the fact that they were cars from Derventa, for example, Modrica, and Odzak, and similar licence plates from Croatia. So for the most part, this happened a day or two after the Serb forces entered those areas. Furthermore, these goods were publicly sold on the streets, and also they were still packaged in the original packaging, products of well-known Bosnian and Croatian firms. And we live in a small town and we know who owns what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My second question would be about illegal weapons in Lisnja. What do you know about it? You started saying that you knew about illegal weapons there. Could you tell us briefly what it was about?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I didn't say there were unregistered weapons there, but the rumours going round town were that certain individuals did have weapons. I didn't confirm that. I don't know how this came about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Those rumours were about what kind and what quantity of weapons?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: In the town itself, since Lisnja is 12 kilometres away, people said that individuals in Lisnja from purchasing weapons, allegedly to defend themselves with. And those stories were going round town at the time. Now, what the quantity of these weapons were and what types of weapons, nobody knew. As I say, this is 12 kilometres away on the road to Banja Luka. We couldn't see it from the town ourselves, nor did we know what was actually going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know whether they were ever formally seized at a later stage or ...

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: I have to say -- I have to tell you what the rumours were in the town of Prnjavor afterwards. What was said was that a member of the JNA had sold the weapons to individuals in Lisnja and that then they went to those houses and looked for those same weapons, the weapons that were sold to these people. Those were the rumours going round Prnjavor. I can't confirm them. But allegedly the members of the JNA sold the weapons and they knew who to go to look for the weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then a final question on the -- I would say the legal papers on your not responding to the mobilisation call. I do see from these papers that you had a defence, not having received the mobilisation papers in time. But even when you received them, that you did not respond to them also. Was there any discussion about whether this mobilisation call, apart from whether you liked the purposes of it at that time, about the legality of that mobilisation call?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: That is a legal question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just stop you. Let me -- my question was whether there was any discussion about it. I'm -- perhaps I would ask you what this discussion was about, but you could also understand the question whether you ever raised the legality or constitutionality or -- of this call. Because I do not see this reflected in the papers, and I'd like to now know whether it was raised; yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't raise that discussion. But before the court, in a discussion, it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems there is a problem with the ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is somebody saying something about a guitar, apparently. As I was saying, during the court proceedings, I talked about the legality or illegality of the call-up, and I think that you can find a legal document in which this can be seen. But I didn't discuss the legitimacy of the call-up anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From what I saw, at least in the first decision, it does not appear as one of the defences you have put to that court. Then I have another question. I saw in the statement of the reasons -- let me just find it. Yes. The statement of reasons given by the municipal misdemeanours court of Prnjavor municipality, at the very end, it says that you -- I'm afraid I took the wrong document. In a document which is a statement, in which a decision is given on your appeal on the ruling, which is a statement by Misdemeanours Judge Zdravko Bunic, at the end, in the legal remedy, it says: "An appeal may be lodged against this Ruling with --" and initially, but still readable -- "the Republican Misdemeanours Court," which is corrected in the "Misdemeanour Chamber in Banja Luka." I understood that you are a lawyer. Could you explain what is the difference between the republican misdemeanour court and what is the misdemeanour chamber in Banja Luka and whether this change in this language was just a practicality or whether it has a further meaning.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: It has a very vital meaning. In the legal proceedings, first of all, I had the right to appeal in the first instance. And then the first-instance ruling was put ad acta [phoen] and a regular proceedings moved. And when the final ruling was brought about, according to the provisions, I had the right to appeal to the misdemeanours court in Sarajevo. So they were the positive legal provisions. Of course, you'll see that this is -- we're dealing with October 1982 [as interpreted] when the Serbian authorities were setting up paramilitary institutions and it was precisely this court in Banja Luka which was the parallel institution. Because, had we wanted to, we couldn't have contacted Sarajevo in any way whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I understand that so, therefore, where, under normal circumstances, you would have had an appeal on the republican misdemeanours court, that now your appeal was to be heard by the misdemeanour chamber in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely right, just as you put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for these answers. Do the questions by the Bench raise any further need for questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours questions do not raise any issues for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: I've just got one question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Karagiannakis has one more question for you. Further examination by Ms. Karagiannakis:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's just a confirmation on what's contained in the legal papers. For failure to answer the mobilisation call, I understand the legal remedies in this paper are fine and imprisonment; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Legal remedies or -- because legal remedies are usually understood to be the possibility to appeal or asking for review.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should say the legal sanctions that flowed from your failure to answer the mobilisation call were first a fine and then a term of imprisonment; right?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: A fine was turned into a prison term, in view of the fact that I hadn't paid the fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was not part of the legal remedy in your case that you would be, for example, dismissed from private employment and have the associated loss of an apartment?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. For failure to respond to the mobilisation, everybody could have been fined, in money terms, and in some drastic cases, a term in prison. But the accompanying punishment of dismissing somebody from their employment and a loss of apartment would have been nonsense, outside any legal system and an expression of the anarchy that set in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KARAGIANNAKIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Odobasic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to understand exactly the -- yes. Yes. Did I understand your answer well, and I hope I did understand the question as well, that the legal remedy would not cover any of the, I would say, side effects of not responding to the mobilisation call, such as losing employment, et cetera? Is that the gist of the question, and did I understand your answer well?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC
